title: Why Do Police Read You Your Rights? #Shorts
description:
Police read you your rights — and it isn't out of politeness.

Decades ago, you could be questioned alone for hours, with no warning at all. Cornered, some people confessed to things they never did.

In 1966, in Miranda v. Arizona, the Supreme Court drew a line: before questioning someone in custody, police must warn them of their rights — to stay silent, and to a lawyer.

It isn't a courtesy. It's a fix built into the system. Without the warning, a confession can be thrown out of court. A few seconds changed every arrest in America.

Watch the full story on the channel.
